title: Book 6, Chapter 20 — Seventeenth and Eighteenth Years of the War—Inaction of the Athenian Army—Alcibiades at Sparta—Investment of Syracuse
paragraphs: The Athenian generals left in Sicily now divided the armament into two parts and drew lots for them, each taking one. With the whole force they sailed for Selinus and Egesta. They wanted to know whether the Egestaeans would give the money, and to look into the question of Selinus and learn how the quarrel between her and Egesta stood. They coasted along Sicily with the shore on their left, on the side facing the Tyrrhene Gulf, and put in at Himera, the only Hellenic city in that part of the island. Admission was refused, and they resumed their voyage. On the way they captured Hyccara, a small Sicanian seaport that was nevertheless at war with Egesta. They enslaved the inhabitants and handed the town over to the Egestaeans, some of whose horse had joined them. The army then went on through the territory of the Sicels until it reached Catana, while the fleet sailed along the coast with the slaves on board. Meanwhile Nicias sailed straight from Hyccara along the coast to Egesta, where he transacted his other business and received thirty talents, and then rejoined the forces. They now sold their slaves for one hundred and twenty talents. Then they sailed around to their Sicel allies to urge them to send troops, and meanwhile went with half of their own force against Hybla in the territory of Gela, a hostile town, but did not succeed in taking it.

Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, the Athenians at once began preparing to move on Syracuse, and the Syracusans on their side prepared to march against them. At first the Syracusans had feared and expected an immediate attack, and the Athenians had not made one. From that moment every day that passed did something to restore their courage. They saw the Athenians sail far away to the other side of Sicily, and go to Hybla only to fail in their attempt to storm it. They therefore thought less of them than ever. As the multitude is apt to do in its moments of confidence, they called on their generals to lead them to Catana, since the enemy would not come to them. Syracusan horse, out reconnoitering, also kept riding up to the Athenian armament. Among other insults, they asked whether the Athenians had really come to settle in a foreign country with the Syracusans, rather than to resettle the Leontines in their own.

The Athenian generals knew of this. They decided to draw the Syracusans out in a mass as far as possible from the city, and in the meantime to sail along the shore by night and take up a convenient position at their leisure. They knew they could not do this so well if they had to disembark from their ships in front of a force that was ready for them, or to advance openly by land. The Syracusans had numerous cavalry, which the Athenians themselves lacked, and it would then be able to do the greatest damage to their light troops and to the crowd that followed them. By this plan, however, they could take up a position where the horse could do them no harm worth speaking of. Some Syracusan exiles with the army had told them of the spot near the Olympieum, which they afterwards occupied. To carry out this idea, the generals devised the following stratagem. They sent to Syracuse a man who was devoted to them, and whom the Syracusan generals thought to be no less in their own interest. He was a native of Catana, and said he came from men in that place whose names the Syracusan generals knew, and whom they knew to be among their supporters still left in the city. He told them that the Athenians spent the night in the town, at some distance from their arms. If the Syracusans would name a day and come with all their people at daybreak to attack the armament, then he and his friends would shut the gates on the troops in the city and set fire to the ships, while the Syracusans would easily take the camp by an attack on the stockade. Many of the Catanians, he said, would help them in this: they were already prepared to act, and he himself had come from them.

The Syracusan generals did not lack confidence, and even without this message they had intended to march on Catana. They believed the man without any adequate inquiry, fixed a day on which they would be there, and dismissed him. The Selinuntines and other allies had now arrived, and the generals gave orders for all the Syracusans to march out in a mass. When their preparations were complete and the time fixed for their arrival was near, they set out for Catana and spent the night on the river Symaethus, in the Leontine territory. The Athenians, as soon as they learned of the approach, took all their forces, together with the Sicels and others who had joined them, put them on board their ships and boats, and sailed by night to Syracuse. So when morning broke the Athenians were landing opposite the Olympieum, ready to seize their camping ground. The Syracusan horse had ridden up first to Catana and found that the whole armament had put to sea. They turned back and told the infantry, and then all turned back together and went to relieve the city.

Meanwhile the Syracusans had a long march before them, and the Athenians quietly settled their army in a convenient position. From there they could begin an engagement whenever they pleased, and the Syracusan cavalry would have the least opportunity of harassing them, either before or during the action. On one side they were fenced off by walls, houses, trees and a marsh, and on the other by cliffs. They also cut down the neighboring trees and carried them to the sea, where they built a palisade alongside their ships. With stones they picked up and wood they raised in haste, they built a fort at Daskon, the most vulnerable point of their position, and they broke down the bridge over the Anapus. The city did nothing to interrupt these preparations. The first hostile force to appear was the Syracusan cavalry, and later all the foot came up together. At first they came close up to the Athenian army. Then, finding that the Athenians did not offer to engage, they crossed the Helorine road and encamped for the night.

The next day the Athenians and their allies prepared for battle, with the following dispositions. The Argives and Mantineans held the right wing, the Athenians the center, and the other allies the rest of the line. Half of the army was drawn up eight deep in front. The other half was drawn up close to the tents in a hollow square, also eight deep, with orders to watch for any troops that were hardest pressed and be ready to support them. The camp followers were placed inside this reserve. The Syracusans, for their part, formed their heavy infantry sixteen deep. It consisted of the mass levy of their own people and the allies who had joined them, the strongest contingent being that of the Selinuntines. Next to them came the cavalry of the Geloans, two hundred in all, with about twenty horse and fifty archers from Camarina. The cavalry, a full twelve hundred strong, was posted on their right, and next to it came the darters. As the Athenians were about to begin the attack, Nicias went along the lines and addressed these words of encouragement to the army and to the nations that made it up:

“Soldiers, men like ourselves, who are here to fight in the same battle, have little need of a long exhortation. To my thinking, the force itself is better fitted to inspire confidence than a fine speech delivered to a weak army. We have Argives, Mantineans, Athenians and the first of the islanders in the ranks together. With so many and so brave companions in arms, it would be strange indeed if we did not feel confident of victory. This is all the more so because we have mass levies opposed to our picked troops, and, what is more, Siceliots, who may disdain us but will not stand against us, since their skill is not at all equal to their rashness. You may also remember that we are far from home and have no friendly land near, except what your own swords shall win you. Here I put before you a motive just the reverse of the one the enemy appeals to. Their cry is that they will fight for their country. Mine is that we will fight for a country that is not ours, where we must conquer or hardly get away, since their horse will be upon us in great numbers. Remember, therefore, your renown, and go boldly against the enemy, and think the present strait and necessity more terrible than they are.”

After this address Nicias at once led the army forward. The Syracusans were not expecting an immediate engagement at that moment, and some had even gone away to the town, which was close by. These now ran up as hard as they could and, though late, took their places here and there in the main body as fast as they joined it. Certainly, neither in this battle nor in the others was the fault of the Syracusans a want of zeal or daring. They were not inferior in courage, so far as their military science could carry them, but when that failed them they were forced to give up their resolution also. On this occasion they had not supposed that the Athenians would begin the attack, and they were forced to stand on their defense at short notice. Even so, they at once took up their arms and advanced to meet them. First the stone-throwers, slingers and archers of both armies began skirmishing, and routed or were routed by one another, as might be expected between light troops. Next, soothsayers brought forward the usual victims, and trumpeters urged on the heavy infantry to the charge. So they advanced. The Syracusans fought for their country, and each individual for his safety that day and his liberty hereafter. In the enemy’s army, the Athenians fought to make another’s country theirs and to save their own from suffering by their defeat. The Argives and the independent allies fought to help them get what they had come for, and to earn by victory another sight of the country they had left behind. The subject allies owed most of their ardor to the desire for self-preservation, which they could hope for only if victorious. Next to this, as a secondary motive, came the chance of serving on easier terms after helping the Athenians to a fresh conquest.

The armies now came to close quarters and for a long while fought without either giving ground. Meanwhile there were some claps of thunder, with lightning and heavy rain. These added to the fears of the side that was fighting for the first time and was very little acquainted with war. To their more experienced adversaries the storm seemed to be caused by the time of year, and they felt much more alarm at the continued resistance of the enemy. At last the Argives drove in the Syracusan left, and after them the Athenians routed the troops opposed to them. The Syracusan army was thus cut in two and took to flight. The Athenians did not pursue far, because the numerous and undefeated Syracusan horse held them in check. These attacked and drove back any of the heavy infantry whom they saw pursuing ahead of the rest. In spite of this, the victors followed as far as was safe while keeping together, and then went back and set up a trophy. Meanwhile the Syracusans rallied at the Helorine road, where they re-formed as well as they could in the circumstances. They even sent a garrison of their own citizens to the Olympieum, fearing that the Athenians might lay hands on some of the treasures there. The rest returned to the town.

The Athenians, however, did not go to the temple. They collected their dead and laid them on a pyre, and spent the night on the field. The next day they gave the enemy back their dead under truce, about two hundred and sixty of the Syracusans and their allies. They gathered up the bones of their own dead, some fifty Athenians and allies, took the spoils of the enemy, and sailed back to Catana. It was now winter. For the moment it did not seem possible to carry on the war before Syracuse. Horse had first to be sent for from Athens and levied among the allies in Sicily, to remove their utter inferiority in cavalry. Money had to be collected in the country and received from Athens. Some of the cities, which they hoped would be more willing to listen to them after the battle, had to be brought over. And corn and all other necessaries had to be provided for a campaign against Syracuse in the spring.

With this in mind they sailed off to Naxos and Catana for the winter. The Syracusans, meanwhile, burned their dead and held an assembly. Hermocrates, son of Hermon, came forward. He was a man of the first order of general ability, and in the war he had shown both military capacity and brilliant courage. He encouraged them and told them not to give way because of what had happened. Their spirit had not been conquered; the harm had come from their lack of discipline. They had not even been beaten by as much as might have been expected, particularly since they were, one might say, novices in the art of war, an army of artisans facing the most practiced soldiers in Hellas. Great harm had also come from the number of generals (there were fifteen of them) and the quantity of orders given, together with the disorder and insubordination of the troops. But suppose they had a few skilled generals, and spent this winter preparing their heavy infantry: finding arms for those who had none, so as to make them as numerous as possible, and compelling them all to attend to their training. Then they would have every chance of beating their adversaries. Courage was already theirs, and discipline in the field would now be added to it. Both qualities would indeed improve, since danger would drill them in discipline, and the confidence that skill gives would lead their courage to surpass itself. The generals should be few and elected with full powers, and an oath should be taken to leave them complete discretion in their command. If they adopted this plan, their secrets would be better kept, all preparations would be properly made, and there would be no room for excuses.

The Syracusans heard him out and voted everything as he advised. They elected three generals: Hermocrates himself, Heraclides, son of Lysimachus, and Sicanus, son of Execestes. They also sent envoys to Corinth and Lacedaemon to obtain a force of allies to join them. The envoys were to persuade the Lacedaemonians to take up the war against the Athenians openly and in real earnest, for the Syracusans’ sake, so that the Athenians might either have to leave Sicily or be less able to send reinforcements to their army there.

The Athenian forces at Catana now at once sailed against Messina, expecting it to be betrayed to them. The intrigue, however, came to nothing after all. Alcibiades was in the secret, and when he left his command on the summons from home, he foresaw that he would be outlawed and gave information of the plot to the friends of the Syracusans in Messina. They at once put its authors to death, and now rose in arms against the opposite faction with those who thought as they did, and succeeded in preventing the admission of the Athenians. After thirteen days of waiting, exposed to the weather, without provisions and with no success, the Athenians went back to Naxos. There they made places for their ships to lie in, put a palisade around their camp, and retired into winter quarters. Meanwhile they sent a galley to Athens for money and for cavalry to join them in the spring. During the winter the Syracusans built a wall onto the city, so as to take in the statue of Apollo Temenites, all along the side looking toward Epipolae. This was to make the task of circumvallation longer and more difficult, in case they were defeated. They also built a fort at Megara and another in the Olympieum, and set palisades along the sea wherever there was a landing place. Meanwhile, knowing that the Athenians were wintering at Naxos, they marched with all their people to Catana, ravaged the land, set fire to the tents and encampment of the Athenians, and returned home. They also learned that the Athenians were sending an embassy to Camarina, on the strength of the alliance concluded in the time of Laches, to win that city over if possible, and they sent another from Syracuse to oppose it. They had a shrewd suspicion that the Camarinaeans had not been very willing in sending what they did send for the first battle. They now feared that the Camarinaeans would refuse to assist them at all in future, after seeing the Athenian success in the action, and would join the Athenians on the strength of their old friendship. Hermocrates, with some others, accordingly arrived at Camarina from Syracuse, and Euphemus and others from the Athenians. An assembly of the Camarinaeans was convened, and Hermocrates spoke as follows, hoping to prejudice them against the Athenians:

“Camarinaeans, we did not come on this embassy because we were afraid that the actual forces of the Athenians would frighten you. We were rather afraid that what they would say to you would win you over before you had heard anything from us. They have come to Sicily with the pretext that you know and the intention that we all suspect. In my opinion their aim is less to restore the Leontines to their homes than to drive us from ours. It is out of all reason that they should restore in Sicily the cities that they lay waste in Hellas, or that they should cherish the Leontine Chalcidians because of their Ionian blood and keep in servitude the Euboean Chalcidians, of whom the Leontines are a colony. No: it is the policy that has served them so well in Hellas which is now being tried in Sicily. The Athenians were chosen as the leaders of the Ionians and of the other allies of Athenian origin, to punish the Mede. They accused some of failure in military service, some of fighting against each other, and others of whatever else, as the case might be, they could find as a plausible pretext, until they had subdued them all. In short, in the struggle against the Medes the Athenians did not fight for the liberty of the Hellenes, nor the Hellenes for their own liberty. The Athenians fought to make their countrymen serve them instead of the Mede, and the Hellenes to change one master for another, wiser indeed than the first, but wiser for evil.

“But we have not now come to declare, to an audience already familiar with them, the misdeeds of a state so open to accusation as the Athenian. We have come much rather to blame ourselves. We have the warning of the Hellenes in those parts who have been enslaved through not supporting each other. We see the same sophisms now being tried on ourselves, such as restoring Leontine kinsfolk and supporting Egestaean allies. Yet we do not stand together and resolutely show them that here are no Ionians, or Hellespontines, or islanders, who change continually but always serve a master, sometimes the Mede and sometimes some other. Here are free Dorians from independent Peloponnese, dwelling in Sicily. Or are we waiting until we are taken in detail, one city after another? We know that in no other way can we be conquered, and we see that they turn to this plan: to divide some of us by words, to draw others by the bait of an alliance into open war with each other, and to ruin others by whatever flattery different circumstances may make acceptable. And do we fancy that when destruction first overtakes a distant fellow countryman, the danger will not come to each of us also, or that he who suffers before us will suffer in himself alone?

“As for the Camarinaean who says that it is the Syracusan, not he, who is the enemy of the Athenian, and who thinks it hard to have to face danger on behalf of my country, I would have him bear in mind that he will fight in my country not more for mine than for his own. He will fight by so much the more safely because he will enter the struggle not alone, after the way has been cleared by my ruin, but with me as his ally. And the object of the Athenian is not so much to punish the enmity of the Syracusan as to use me as a blind to secure the friendship of the Camarinaean. Then there is the man who envies or even fears us (and great powers must always be envied and feared), and who on this account wishes Syracuse to be humbled to teach us a lesson, but would still have her survive, in the interest of his own security. The wish he indulges is not humanly possible. A man can control his own desires, but he cannot likewise control circumstances. If his calculations prove mistaken, he may live to bewail his own misfortune, and wish to be again envying my prosperity. That wish will be idle if he now sacrifices us and refuses to take his share of dangers which are the same, in reality though not in name, for him as for us. What is nominally the preservation of our power is really his own salvation. It was to be expected that you of all people in the world, Camarinaeans, being our immediate neighbors and next in danger, would have foreseen this. Instead of supporting us in the lukewarm way that you are doing now, you would rather have come to us of your own accord. You would now be offering at Syracuse the aid which you would have asked for at Camarina, if the Athenians had come first to Camarina, to encourage us to resist the invader. Neither you, however, nor the rest have yet bestirred yourselves in this direction.

“Perhaps fear will make you anxious to do right by both us and the invaders, and you will plead your alliance with the Athenians. But you did not make that alliance against your friends. You made it against any enemies who might attack you, and to help the Athenians when others wronged them, not when, as now, they themselves are wronging their neighbors. Even the Rhegians, who are Chalcidians, refuse to help restore the Chalcidian Leontines. It would be strange if they see the point of this fine pretense and are wise without any reason, while you, with every reason on your side, still chose to assist your natural enemies. It would be strange if you joined their direst foes to undo those whom nature has made your own kinsfolk. That is not to do right. You should rather help us, and not fear their armament. It has no terrors if we hold together; it is formidable only if we let them succeed in separating us. Even when they attacked us on our own and won a battle, they had to go away without achieving their purpose.

“United, therefore, we have no cause to despair. We have fresh encouragement to league together, the more so since help will come to us from the Peloponnesians, who are beyond doubt the superiors of the Athenians in military matters. And do not suppose that your prudent policy of taking neither side, because you are allies of both, is either safe for you or fair to us. In practice it is not as fair as it pretends. If you refuse to join us, the vanquished is defeated and the victor conquers. What does your abstention do but leave the one to perish unaided and allow the other to do wrong unhindered? Yet it would be more honorable to join those who are not only the injured party but your own kindred. By doing so you would defend the common interests of Sicily and keep your friends the Athenians from doing wrong.

“To conclude: we Syracusans say that it is useless to demonstrate to you or to the rest what you already know as well as we do. But we entreat you, and if our entreaty fails, we protest. We are menaced by our eternal enemies the Ionians, and we are betrayed by you, our fellow Dorians. If the Athenians reduce us, your decision will have given them the victory, yet they will take the honor in their own name. The prize of their triumph will be the very men who enabled them to win it. If, on the other hand, we are the conquerors, you will pay for having been the cause of our danger. Consider, then, and choose now: either the security that present servitude offers, or the prospect of conquering with us, and so escaping a disgraceful submission to an Athenian master and the lasting enmity of Syracuse.”
Such were the words of Hermocrates. After him Euphemus, the Athenian ambassador, spoke as follows:

“We came here only to renew the former alliance. But the attack of the Syracusans forces us to speak of our empire and of the good right we have to it. The speaker himself gave the best proof of this when he called the Ionians the eternal enemies of the Dorians. So they are. The Peloponnesian Dorians outnumbered us and were our next neighbors, and we Ionians looked for the best means of escaping their domination. After the Median War we had a fleet, and with it we shook off the empire and supremacy of the Lacedaemonians. They had no more right to give orders to us than we to them, except that at that moment they were the strongest. We were appointed leaders of the King’s former subjects, and we remain so. We think we are least likely to fall under the dominion of the Peloponnesians if we have a force to defend ourselves with. And in strict truth we did nothing unfair in reducing to subjection the Ionians and islanders, the kinsfolk whom the Syracusans say we have enslaved. Our kinsfolk came against their mother country, that is to say against us, together with the Mede. They lacked the courage to revolt and sacrifice their property, as we did when we abandoned our city. They chose to be slaves themselves, and to try to make slaves of us.

“We deserve to rule, therefore, because we put the largest fleet and an unflinching patriotism at the service of the Hellenes, and because these, our subjects, harmed us by their ready subservience to the Medes. Apart from desert, we also seek to strengthen ourselves against the Peloponnesians. We make no fine claim to a right to rule on the ground that we overthrew the barbarian single-handed, or that we ran the risks we ran for the freedom of the subjects in question any more than for that of all, and for our own. No one can be blamed for providing for his own safety. If we are now here in Sicily, it is likewise in the interest of our security, and we see that your interest coincides with it. We prove this by the very conduct which the Syracusans bring against us and which you suspect a little too timidly. We know that those whom fear has made suspicious may be carried away for the moment by the charm of eloquence, but that when it comes to action they follow their interests.

“Now, as we have said, fear makes us hold our empire in Hellas, and fear now brings us here, with the help of our friends, to settle matters safely in Sicily. We do not come to enslave anyone, but rather to prevent anyone from being enslaved. Meanwhile, let no one imagine that we concern ourselves with you when you have nothing to do with us. If you are preserved and able to hold out against the Syracusans, they will be less likely to harm us by sending troops to the Peloponnesians. In this way you have everything to do with us, and for this reason it is perfectly reasonable for us to restore the Leontines. We would make them not subjects, like their kinsmen in Euboea, but as powerful as possible, so that they may help us by harassing the Syracusans from their frontier. In Hellas we alone are a match for our enemies. As for the claim that it is out of all reason for us to free the Sicilian while we enslave the Chalcidian, the fact is that the Chalcidian is useful to us because he is without arms and contributes only money, while the Leontines and our other friends here cannot be too independent.

“Besides, for tyrants and imperial cities nothing is unreasonable if it is expedient, and no one is a kinsman unless he can be trusted. Friendship or enmity everywhere depends on time and circumstance. Here in Sicily our interest is not to weaken our friends, but to use their strength to cripple our enemies. Why doubt this? In Hellas we treat our allies according to their usefulness to us. The Chians and Methymnians govern themselves and supply ships. Most of the rest are on harder terms and pay tribute in money. Others, although they are islanders and easy for us to take, are entirely free, because they hold convenient positions around Peloponnese. So in settling the affairs of the states here in Sicily, we should naturally be guided by our interest, and by fear of the Syracusans, as we have said. They aim to rule you. Their plan is to use the suspicions we arouse to unite you, and then, when we have gone away having accomplished nothing, to become the masters of Sicily, by force or because you stand alone. And masters they must become if you unite with them. A force of that size, once united, would be no longer easy for us to deal with, and as soon as we were gone they would be more than a match for you.

“Any other view of the case is refuted by the facts. When you first invited us over, the fear you held out was danger to Athens if we let you fall under the dominion of Syracuse. It is not right now to distrust the very argument by which you claimed to convince us, or to give way to suspicion because we have come with a larger force against the power of that city. The people you should really distrust are the Syracusans. We cannot stay here without you. And if we proved treacherous enough to bring you into subjection, we should be unable to keep you in bondage, because of the length of the voyage and the difficulty of guarding cities that are large and, in a military sense, continental. The Syracusans, by contrast, live close to you, not in a camp but in a city greater than the force we have with us. They plot against you always, and never let slip an opportunity once offered, as they have shown in the case of the Leontines and others. And now they have the effrontery, as if you were fools, to invite you to help them against the power that stands in their way and has so far kept Sicily independent. We, against them, invite you to a much more real safety. We beg you not to betray the common safety that each of us has in the other. Consider that they, even without allies, will always have the way open to you because of their numbers, while you will not often have the chance of defending yourselves with such numerous auxiliaries. If through your suspicions you once let these go away unsuccessful or defeated, you will long to see even a handful of them back again, when the day is past in which their presence could do anything for you.

“But we hope, Camarinaeans, that the slanders of the Syracusans will not be allowed to succeed either with you or with the rest. We have told you the whole truth about the things we are suspected of, and we will now briefly sum it up, in the hope of convincing you. We assert that we are rulers in Hellas so that we may not be subjects, and liberators in Sicily so that we may not be harmed by the Sicilians. We are compelled to interfere in many things, because we have many things to guard against. And now, as before, we have come as allies to those of you who suffer wrong in this island, not uninvited but upon invitation. So do not make yourselves judges or censors of our conduct, and do not try to turn us from our course, which it would now be difficult to do. Rather, wherever our interfering policy or our character agrees with your interest, take that and make use of it. Be sure that, far from being injurious to all alike, that policy is even beneficial to most of the Hellenes. Thanks to it, all men in all places, even where we are not, find themselves constrained to be moderate against their will, or to be preserved without trouble of their own. This applies to those who fear aggression and to those who contemplate it. The first have the near prospect of obtaining our intervention in their favor. The second know that our arrival would make the venture dangerous. Do not reject this security, which is open to all who desire it and is now offered to you. Do as others do: instead of always being on the defensive against the Syracusans, unite with us and in your turn at last threaten them.”

Such were the words of Euphemus. The feelings of the Camarinaeans were as follows. They sympathized with the Athenians, except insofar as they might be afraid of their subjugating Sicily, and they had always been at enmity with their neighbor Syracuse. Yet precisely because the Syracusans were their neighbors, they feared them the more of the two. Apprehensive that Syracuse might conquer even without their help, they had first sent the few horsemen already mentioned, and they determined to support Syracuse most in fact for the future, although as sparingly as possible. For the moment, however, so as not to seem to slight the Athenians, especially since the Athenians had been successful in the engagement, they decided to give both sides the same answer. In keeping with this resolution they answered that, as both of the contending parties happened to be their allies, they thought it most consistent with their oaths to side with neither for the present. With this answer the ambassadors of both parties departed.

Meanwhile Syracuse went on with her preparations for war. The Athenians, encamped at Naxos, tried through negotiation to win over as many Sicels as they could. Most of the Sicels in the low country, who were subjects of Syracuse, held aloof. The peoples of the interior, however, had always been independent, and with few exceptions they joined the Athenians at once, bringing corn down to the army and in some cases money as well. Against those who refused, the Athenians marched, and they forced some to join. In other cases the Syracusans sent garrisons and reinforcements and stopped them. The Athenians then moved their winter quarters from Naxos to Catana, rebuilt the camp the Syracusans had burned, and remained there through the rest of the winter. They sent one galley to Carthage with offers of friendship, hoping for some assistance, and another to Tyrrhenia, where some of the cities had offered of their own accord to join them in the war. They also sent messages to the Sicels and to Egesta asking for as many horses as could be had. In the meantime they prepared bricks, iron and everything else needed for the work of circumvallation, intending to open hostilities in the spring.

Meanwhile the Syracusan envoys sent to Corinth and Lacedaemon were working their way along the coast, trying to persuade the Italiots to oppose the Athenians, whose proceedings threatened Italy as much as Syracuse. At Corinth the envoys made a speech asking for help on the ground of their common origin. The Corinthians voted at once to give it themselves, wholeheartedly, and then sent envoys along with them to Lacedaemon to help persuade her too to wage the war on the Athenians more openly at home, and to send succors to Sicily. When the Corinthian envoys reached Lacedaemon, they found Alcibiades there with his fellow refugees. He had crossed at once from Thurii in a trading vessel, first to Cyllene in Elis and then on to Lacedaemon, upon the Lacedaemonians’ own invitation and with a safe conduct obtained first, since he feared them because of his part in the affair of Mantinea. So in the assembly of the Lacedaemonians the Corinthians, the Syracusans and Alcibiades all pressed the same request, and persuaded them. But the ephors and the authorities resolved only to send envoys to Syracuse to stop it from surrendering to the Athenians. They showed no inclination to send any help. Alcibiades then came forward and stirred up and inflamed the Lacedaemonians with the following speech:

“I must first speak to you about the prejudice against me, so that suspicion may not make you unwilling to hear me on public affairs. The connection with you as your proxeni had been renounced by my family’s ancestors out of some discontent. I personally tried to renew it by my good offices toward you, in particular at the time of the disaster at Pylos. Yet although I kept up this friendly attitude, you chose to make the peace with the Athenians through my enemies, and so to strengthen them and discredit me. You had no right, then, to complain when I turned to the Mantineans and Argives and took other opportunities to thwart and injure you. The time has now come for those of you who may have been unfairly angry with me in the bitterness of that moment to see the matter in its true light and take a different view. Others judged me unfavorably because I leaned toward the commons. They should not think their dislike any better founded. We have always been enemies of tyrants, and everyone who opposes arbitrary power is called commons. For that reason we continued as leaders of the multitude. Besides, democracy being the government of the city, in most things we had to conform to existing conditions. Still, we tried to be more moderate than the licentious temper of the times. Others, then as now, tried to lead the multitude astray — the very men who banished me. Our party was that of the whole people. Our creed was to do our part in preserving the form of government under which the city had enjoyed the utmost greatness and freedom, and which we had found in place. As for democracy, the men of sense among us knew what it was, and I perhaps as well as any, since I have more reason to complain of it. But there is nothing new to be said about a patent absurdity. And we did not think it safe to change it while you were pressing us with your hostility.

“So much for the prejudices against me. I can now turn your attention to the questions you must consider, on which my superior knowledge perhaps entitles me to speak. Our purpose in sailing to Sicily was, first, to conquer the Siceliots if possible, then the Italiots too, and finally to attack the empire and city of Carthage. If all or most of these schemes succeeded, we were next to attack Peloponnese. We would bring the whole force of the Hellenes newly gained in those regions, take into our pay a number of barbarians, such as the Iberians and others there, who are admittedly the most warlike known, and build many galleys besides those we already had, since Italy has plenty of timber. With this fleet we would blockade Peloponnese from the sea, while our armies assailed it by land, storming some cities and drawing works of circumvallation around others. In this way we hoped to reduce it without difficulty, and then to rule the whole of the Hellenic name. For the better execution of these plans, the newly acquired places in those countries were to supply money and corn in sufficient quantities, quite apart from our revenues at home.

“You have now heard the history of the present expedition from the man who knows best what our objects were. The remaining generals will carry them out just the same, if they can. Now I will show that the states in Sicily must succumb unless you help them. The Siceliots are inexperienced, but even now they might be saved if their forces were united. The Syracusans alone, however, who have already been beaten in one battle with all their people and are blockaded from the sea, will not be able to hold out against the Athenian armament now there. If Syracuse falls, all Sicily falls with it, and Italy immediately after. Then the danger from that quarter that I mentioned just now will soon be upon you. No one should imagine, therefore, that only Sicily is at stake. Peloponnese is at stake as well, unless you speedily do as I say. Put troops on board ship and send them to Syracuse, men who can row their ships themselves and serve as heavy infantry the moment they land. And what I think even more important than the troops, send a Spartan as commanding officer, to give discipline to the forces already in the field and to compel those who refuse to serve. This will make the friends you already have more confident, and will encourage the waverers to join you. Meanwhile you must make war here more openly, so that the Syracusans, seeing that you have not forgotten them, may take heart to resist, and so that the Athenians may find it harder to reinforce their armament. You must fortify Decelea in Attica. This is the blow the Athenians always fear most, and the only one they think they have not suffered in the present war. The surest way to harm an enemy is to find out what he most fears and attack him by that means, since each man naturally knows his own weak points best and fears accordingly. This fortification will benefit you and create difficulties for your adversaries. I shall pass over many of these and mention only the chief. Most of the property in the country will become yours, by capture or surrender. The Athenians will at once lose their revenue from the silver mines at Laurium, their present gains from their land and from the law courts, and above all the revenue from their allies. That will be paid less regularly, as the allies lose their awe of Athens and see you taking up the war with vigor. How zealously and how quickly all this is done, Lacedaemonians, depends on yourselves. As to its being possible, I am quite confident, and I have little fear of being mistaken.

“Meanwhile I hope that none of you will think the worse of me because I, who until now passed for a lover of my country, am now actively joining its worst enemies to attack it. I hope too that you will not distrust my words as the product of an outlaw’s zeal. I am an outlaw through the iniquity of those who drove me out, but not, if you will be guided by me, from serving you. My worst enemies are not you, who only harmed your foes, but those who forced their friends to turn into enemies. When I am wronged I do not feel love of country. I felt it when I was secure in my rights as a citizen. In fact I do not think I am now attacking a country that is still mine. I am trying instead to win back one that is mine no longer. The true lover of his country is not the one who submits to losing it unjustly instead of attacking it. He is the one whose longing for it is so great that he will stop at nothing to recover it. For myself, Lacedaemonians, I beg you therefore to employ me without scruple in danger and hardship of every kind. Bear in mind the saying that everyone repeats: if I did you great harm as an enemy, I can also do you good service as a friend, since I know the plans of the Athenians and only guessed at yours. And I entreat you to believe, for your own part, that your most vital interests are now being weighed. Send the expeditions to Sicily and Attica without hesitation. With only a small part of your forces present, you will save important cities in that island and destroy the power of Athens, as it is now and as it may become. After that you will live in security and hold the supremacy over all Hellas, resting not on force but on consent and affection.”

Such were the words of Alcibiades. The Lacedaemonians had already intended to march against Athens, but were still waiting and looking around. Now they received this particular information from Alcibiades, whom they regarded as the man who best knew the truth of the matter, and they at once became far more earnest. They turned their attention to fortifying Decelea and to sending immediate help to the Sicilians. They appointed Gylippus, son of Cleandridas, to command the Syracusans, and told him to confer with that people and with the Corinthians and to arrange for succors to reach the island by the best and quickest means that circumstances allowed. Gylippus asked the Corinthians to send two ships at once to Asine, and to make ready the rest that they meant to send, so that they could sail at the right time. When this was settled, the envoys left Lacedaemon.

In the meantime the Athenian galley that the generals had sent for money and cavalry arrived from Sicily. The Athenians heard their requests and voted to send the supplies for the armament and the cavalry. So the winter ended, and with it the seventeenth year of the present war of which Thucydides is the historian.

The next summer, at the very start of the season, the Athenians in Sicily set out from Catana and sailed along the coast to Megara in Sicily. As I have mentioned above, the Syracusans had driven out the inhabitants of Megara in the time of their tyrant Gelo and occupied the territory themselves. The Athenians landed there and laid waste the country. Their attack on a Syracusan fort failed, and they went on with the fleet and army to the river Terias. They advanced inland, laid waste the plain and set fire to the corn. They encountered a small Syracusan party and killed some of it, then set up a trophy and returned to their ships. Sailing back to Catana, they took in provisions there. Then, with their whole force, they went against Centoripa, a town of the Sicels, took it by capitulation, and left, having also burned the corn of the Inessaeans and Hybleans. When they got back to Catana, they found that the horsemen had come from Athens: two hundred and fifty, with their equipment but without horses, which were to be procured on the spot, along with thirty mounted archers and three hundred talents of silver.

The same spring the Lacedaemonians marched against Argos. They got as far as Cleonae, when an earthquake occurred and they turned back. After this the Argives invaded the Thyreatid, on their border, and carried off much booty from the Lacedaemonians, which sold for no less than twenty-five talents. The same summer, not long afterward, the Thespian commons attacked the party in office. The attack failed, because help came from Thebes. Some of the attackers were caught, and others took refuge at Athens.

The same summer the Syracusans learned that the Athenians had been joined by their cavalry and were about to march against them. They realized that, even if the Athenians won a battle, they could not easily invest the city without becoming masters of Epipolae, a steep height directly over the town. They therefore resolved to guard its approaches, so that the enemy could not climb up unobserved by the only way up. The rest of the height is high ground that drops straight down to the city and is all visible from inside. Since it lies above everything else, the Syracusans call the place Epipolae, or Overtown. At daybreak they went out in a body to the meadow along the river Anapus. Their new generals, Hermocrates and his colleagues, had just taken office. They reviewed the heavy infantry and first picked from it six hundred men under Diomilus, an exile from Andros. This force was to guard Epipolae and to muster at a moment’s notice to give help wherever it was needed.

The Athenians, meanwhile, were holding a review that very same morning. They had already landed unobserved from Catana with the whole armament, opposite a place called Leon, not much more than half a mile from Epipolae. There they put the army ashore and anchored the fleet at Thapsus, a peninsula that runs out into the sea and is joined to the land by a narrow isthmus. It is not far from the city of Syracuse by land or by water. The Athenian naval force built a stockade across the isthmus and stayed quietly at Thapsus. The land army ran straight to Epipolae and climbed up by Euryelus before the Syracusans noticed, or could come up from the meadow and the review. Diomilus with his six hundred and the others hurried as fast as they could, but they had nearly three miles to go from the meadow before they reached the Athenians. They attacked in considerable disorder and were defeated in battle at Epipolae. They withdrew to the town having lost about three hundred men, Diomilus among them. After this the Athenians set up a trophy and gave the Syracusans back their dead under truce. The next day they went down to Syracuse itself, and when no one came out against them, they climbed back up and built a fort at Labdalum, at the edge of the cliffs of Epipolae facing Megara. It was to serve as a magazine for their baggage and money whenever they advanced to battle or went to work on the lines.

Not long afterward three hundred cavalry joined them from Egesta, and about a hundred from the Sicels, Naxians and others. Adding the two hundred and fifty from Athens, for whom they had obtained horses from the Egestaeans and Catanians and bought others, they now had six hundred and fifty cavalry altogether. They posted a garrison in Labdalum and advanced to Syca, where they encamped and rapidly built the Circle, the center of their wall of circumvallation. The Syracusans were appalled at how fast the work was going. They resolved to go out, give battle and interrupt it. The two armies were already drawn up for battle when the Syracusan generals saw that their men were having such trouble forming a line, and were in such disorder, that they led them back into the town, all but part of the cavalry. This cavalry stayed behind and prevented the Athenians from carrying stones or scattering any great distance. Then one tribe of the Athenian heavy infantry, with all the cavalry, charged and routed the Syracusan horse, inflicting some loss. The Athenians set up a trophy for this cavalry action.

The next day the Athenians began to build the wall north of the Circle, while gathering stone and timber and laying it down toward Trogilus along the shortest line for their works from the great harbor to the sea. The Syracusans, under the guidance of their generals and above all Hermocrates, resolved to risk no more general engagements. They decided instead to build a counterwork across the line where the Athenians were going to carry their wall. If it could be finished in time, the enemy’s lines would be cut. If he tried to interrupt them by an attack, they would send part of their forces against him and secure the approaches beforehand with their stockade, while the Athenians would have to stop working with their whole force to deal with them. So they sallied out and began to build. Starting from their city, they ran a cross wall below the Athenian Circle, cutting down the olive trees and putting up wooden towers. The Athenian fleet had not yet sailed around into the great harbor, so the Syracusans still held the seacoast, and the Athenians were bringing their provisions overland from Thapsus.

The Syracusans now judged the stockades and stonework of their counterwall far enough advanced. The Athenians were afraid of dividing their forces and fighting at a disadvantage, and were busy with their own wall, so they did not come out to interrupt. The Syracusans left one tribe to guard the new work and went back into the city. Meanwhile the Athenians destroyed the pipes that carried their drinking-water underground into the city. They waited until the rest of the Syracusans were in their tents at midday, some had even gone off into the city, and the men in the stockade were keeping only a poor guard. Then they appointed three hundred picked men of their own, together with some picked from the light troops and armed for the purpose, to rush suddenly at full speed to the counterwork. The rest of the army advanced in two divisions: one under one of the generals toward the city, in case of a sortie, the other under the other general toward the stockade at the postern gate. The three hundred attacked and took the stockade, which its garrison had abandoned. The garrison took refuge in the outworks around the statue of Apollo Temenites. The pursuers broke in after them, but once inside they were driven out by the Syracusans, and a few Argives and Athenians were killed. After this the whole army withdrew. They tore down the counterwork, pulled up the stockade, took the stakes to their own lines, and set up a trophy.

The next day the Athenians at the Circle began fortifying the cliff above the marsh, which on this side of Epipolae faces the great harbor. This was also the shortest line for their work to run down across the plain and the marsh to the harbor. Meanwhile the Syracusans marched out and began a second stockade, starting from the city and crossing the middle of the marsh. Alongside it they dug a trench, so that the Athenians could not carry their wall down to the sea. As soon as the Athenians had finished their work at the cliff, they attacked the Syracusan stockade and ditch again. They ordered the fleet to sail around from Thapsus into the great harbor of Syracuse, and at about dawn went down from Epipolae into the plain. They laid doors and planks over the marsh where it was muddy but firmest, crossed on these, and by daybreak had taken the ditch and the stockade, except for a small part that they took later. A battle followed, and the Athenians won it. The right wing of the Syracusans fled to the town and the left to the river. The three hundred picked Athenians, wanting to cut off the retreat, ran on toward the bridge. The Syracusans, alarmed, and with most of their cavalry beside them, closed with these men and routed them, driving them back on the Athenian right wing, and the first tribe of that wing was thrown into a panic by the shock. Seeing this, Lamachus came to help from the Athenian left with a few archers and the Argives. He crossed a ditch and found himself isolated with a few who had crossed with him, and he was killed along with five or six of them. The Syracusans hastily snatched up these bodies and got them across the river to safety, and themselves retreated as the rest of the Athenian army came up.

Meanwhile the men who had at first fled to the city saw how things were turning. They rallied from the town and formed up against the Athenians in front of them. They also sent part of their number against the Circle on Epipolae, which they hoped to take while it was empty of defenders. They captured and destroyed the Athenian outwork of a thousand feet, but the Circle itself was saved by Nicias. Illness had kept him there, and he ordered the servants to set fire to the engines and the timber lying in front of the wall. He knew that for lack of men there was no other way of escape. The result justified this step: the Syracusans, because of the fire, came no closer and retreated. Meanwhile help was arriving from the Athenians below, who had put to flight the troops opposed to them, and the fleet, as ordered, was sailing from Thapsus into the great harbor. When the troops on the heights saw this, they hastily withdrew, and the whole Syracusan army went back into the city, thinking that with their present force they would no longer be able to stop the wall from reaching the sea.

After this the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back the Syracusan dead under truce, receiving in return Lamachus and the men who had fallen with him. With all their forces, naval and military, now present, they began at Epipolae and the cliffs and shut the Syracusans in with a double wall running down to the sea. Provisions for the armament were now brought from all over Italy. Many of the Sicels, who until then had been waiting to see how matters would go, joined the Athenians as allies, and three ships of fifty oars arrived from Tyrrhenia. Everything else was going in line with their hopes. The Syracusans began to despair of saving themselves by arms, as no relief had come to them from Peloponnese. They were now discussing terms of capitulation among themselves and with Nicias, who had become sole commander after the death of Lamachus. Nothing was decided. As was natural for men in difficulty and more closely besieged than before, there was much talk with Nicias and still more in the town. Their present misfortunes had also made them suspicious of one another. The blame for their disasters fell on the ill-fortune or treachery of the generals who had been in command when they happened. These generals were removed, and Heraclides, Eucles and Tellias were elected in their place.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonian Gylippus and the ships from Corinth were off Leucas, intent on hurrying to the relief of Sicily. The reports reaching them were alarming, and all of them agreed on the falsehood that Syracuse was already completely invested. Gylippus gave up hope of Sicily. Wanting to save Italy, he crossed the Ionian Sea quickly to Tarentum, with the Corinthian Pythen, two Laconian vessels and two Corinthian. The Corinthians were to follow him once they had manned, besides their own ten, two Leucadian and two Ambraciot ships. From Tarentum Gylippus first went as an envoy to Thurii and renewed his claim to the rights of citizenship that his father had held. He failed to win over the townspeople, so he weighed anchor and coasted along Italy. Opposite the Terinaean Gulf the wind that blows hard and steadily from the north in that region caught him and carried him out to sea. After very rough weather he returned to Tarentum, where he hauled ashore and repaired the ships that had suffered most in the storm. Nicias heard of his approach, but, like the Thurians, he despised the small number of his ships. He took piracy to be the only likely purpose of the voyage, and so took no precautions for the present.

About the same time in this summer, the Lacedaemonians and their allies invaded Argos and laid waste most of the country. The Athenians went to the relief of the Argives with thirty ships, and in doing so broke their treaty with the Lacedaemonians in the most open manner. Up to then their co-operation with the Argives and Mantineans had gone no further than raids from Pylos and landings on the coast of the rest of Peloponnese rather than on the Laconian coast. The Argives had often begged them to land their heavy infantry in Laconia, if only for a moment, ravage even a little of it with them, and leave, but the Athenians had always refused. Now, under the command of Pythodorus, Laespodius and Demaratus, they landed at Epidaurus Limera, Prasiae and other places and plundered the country. This gave the Lacedaemonians a better pretext for hostilities against Athens. When the Athenians had left Argos with their fleet, and the Lacedaemonians too, the Argives made an incursion into the Phlisaid, ravaged the land, killed some of the inhabitants, and returned home.
